title: Job 41:1–8
context: The LORD continues his second speech to Job from the whirlwind (begun at 40:6), turning from Behemoth to Leviathan with a string of questions: can Job catch, bargain with, tame, sell, or spear this creature (41:1–7)? One encounter would be enough (41:8). The WEB explains Leviathan as a name for a crocodile or similar creature. Other identifications have been proposed, and Leviathan also appears as a sea creature or chaos figure in poetic texts such as Job 3:8, Psalm 74:14, and Isaiah 27:1; some scholars compare older Canaanite sea-monster imagery. These identifications are held with caution here. Versification: English/WEB 41:1–8 is Hebrew 40:25–32, and 41:9–34 is Hebrew 41:1–26; this page keeps the WEB numbering.

verses.text: “Can you draw out Leviathan with a fish hook, or press down his tongue with a cord?
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD asks, “Can you draw out Leviathan with a fish hook?” Arminian readers see the question exposing Job’s limits: a creature he cannot catch is still within the Creator’s rule and knowledge.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the question humbling Job before God’s sovereignty over all creatures. For Leviathan as an enemy of God in Isaiah 27:1, readers can consult the existing box there rather than a new contrast here.

verses.text: Can you put a rope into his nose, or pierce his jaw through with a hook?
verses.arminianNotes: “Can you put a rope into his nose, or pierce his jaw through with a hook?” Arminian readers see the LORD piling up hunter’s questions to show that Job cannot subdue this creature.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a series of questions designed to show human weakness. The point is not to teach techniques of capture but to set Job’s strength beside the strength God has made.

verses.text: Will he make many petitions to you, or will he speak soft words to you?
verses.arminianNotes: “Will he make many petitions to you, or will he speak soft words to you?” Arminian readers hear gentle irony: Leviathan will not plead with Job as a captive pleads with a conqueror.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear irony in the picture of a beast begging for mercy. Readers in this tradition see the LORD teaching Job, through humor and wonder, how small human mastery is.

verses.text: Will he make a covenant with you, that you should take him for a servant forever?
verses.arminianNotes: “Will he make a covenant with you, that you should take him for a servant forever?” Arminian readers see the absurdity of Job binding Leviathan by agreement as a permanent servant.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the impossibility of taming Leviathan by treaty. Readers in this tradition note the contrast with God, who rules this creature without needing any bargain.

verses.text: Will you play with him as with a bird? Or will you bind him for your girls?
verses.arminianNotes: “Will you play with him as with a bird? Or will you bind him for your girls?” Arminian readers see the image of a pet underscoring that Leviathan is no plaything for Job.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see playful irony. Psalm 104:26 pictures leviathan at play in the sea God made, and readers in this tradition note that what is fearsome to Job is not fearsome to God.

verses.text: Will traders barter for him? Will they part him among the merchants?
verses.arminianNotes: “Will traders barter for him? Will they part him among the merchants?” Arminian readers see the LORD asking whether Leviathan could become a mere commodity in human trade.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the creature placed beyond human commerce. Readers in this tradition hear the question pressing home that some parts of creation answer to God alone.

verses.text: Can you fill his skin with barbed irons, or his head with fish spears?
verses.arminianNotes: “Can you fill his skin with barbed irons, or his head with fish spears?” Arminian readers see weapons of the hunt shown to be useless, preparing for the fuller description of the creature’s armor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see human weapons set against the creature’s strength. The questions continue to show Job that he lacks the power he would need to govern the world he questions.

verses.text: Lay your hand on him. Remember the battle, and do so no more.
verses.arminianNotes: “Lay your hand on him. Remember the battle, and do so no more.” Arminian readers see a sober warning that one encounter would be enough to teach caution and humility.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear a warning against presumption. Readers in this tradition see the verse preparing for the LORD’s argument that if Leviathan cannot be faced, how much less can God be challenged.
